> **What this case shows** — an ADL/IADL questionnaire is scored by *summing*
> ordinal items, but a raw sum is **not** an interval measure: moving a Barthel
> total from 40 to 50 is not the same real gain as 90 to 100. A **polytomous
> Rasch (Partial Credit) model** fixes this — it converts the ordered-category
> responses to an **interval (logit) scale** and ranks the items by the ability
> each demands. On real polytomous data the ecosystem's dependency-free engine
> reproduces the reference implementation (**eRm**, conditional maximum
> likelihood) **exactly** — item and person agreement **r = 1.00** — with a
> person separation reliability of **0.86**. **What reproduces, and what
> doesn't** — the item hierarchy and the person measures reproduce across two
> independent estimators; what does **not** transfer is a universal cut score,
> because the logit scale is anchored to *this* item set (measures compare within
> an instrument, not across, unless co-calibrated). **How to read it** — left,
> the 24 items ranked by difficulty on the logit scale (bars = standard error);
> right, our item locations against eRm's, on the line of identity.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — turn an ordinal scale into a defensible measure in three moves:
**recode** each item's responses to consecutive categories → **fit** the
polytomous Rasch model → **read** the item difficulty hierarchy and the interval
person measures (with per-person standard errors).
**Way of thinking** — do not average ordinal codes as if they were centimetres.
Check that the item hierarchy is *substantively sensible* (a hard item should be
hard to endorse) and that category thresholds are ordered before trusting the
scale; report the person measure's standard error rather than assuming equal
precision at every score.
**Ecosystem usage** — chain one function per role: `raschAnalyze()`
(PhysioClinical) recodes a registered ADL instrument's responses and calls the
engine `pcm_measure()` (PhysioAppKit), which returns the item calibration, the
interval person measures and the fit. The final section shows the same call on a
Barthel/Lawton response matrix.
:::

## Proposition

A raw ADL-scale total is not an interval measure. Fitting a polytomous Rasch
model converts the ordered-category responses to an interval (logit) scale and
ranks the items by the ability each demands. On real polytomous data the
ecosystem's JMLE engine reproduces the reference **eRm** (conditional ML)
calibration essentially exactly — item-location **Spearman and Pearson = 1.00**,
person-measure **Pearson = 1.00** — with a person separation reliability of
**0.86**.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from measurement theory, on data built to test it.** The
`VerbAgg` data (distributed with `lme4`) is the *canonical Partial Credit Model
benchmark*: 316 people rated 24 verbal-aggression situations on a three-category
scale (no / perhaps / yes). It has the **same ordered-category structure as an
ADL/IADL scale** — a set of items, each scored in ordered levels, that together
locate a person on a latent trait — which is exactly why it is the public
stand-in here for a labelled Barthel or Lawton response set. The question the
data was made to answer: can a Rasch model place items and persons on one
interval scale, and does an independent estimator agree?

## Challenge & approach

The difficulty is that ordinal categories are not numbers: the "distance" from
*no* to *perhaps* need not equal *perhaps* to *yes*, and it can differ between
items. The Rasch recipe solves this by estimating, for each item, the latent
locations of its category thresholds, and for each person a single ability, all
on one logit scale. The ecosystem does it with a compact, dependency-free joint
maximum-likelihood estimator (`pcm_measure`); we check it against **eRm**, which
uses a *different* estimator (conditional ML) and codebase, so agreement is
evidence about the method, not a shared bug.

## Data

The **VerbAgg** polytomous item-response data, distributed with the `lme4`
package (De Boeck & Wilson 2004; Bates et al. 2015) — 316 persons × 24
three-category items. The exact matrix used is recorded in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Item difficulty hierarchy on the interval logit scale (left) and cross-tool
agreement of item locations, ours vs eRm (right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* on the left, each item sits at its calibrated difficulty in
logits — higher = harder to endorse; the horizontal bars are ±1 standard error.
On the right, every point is one item's location under our JMLE engine (y) versus
eRm's CML (x); they fall on the identity line.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| item-location agreement (Spearman / Pearson) vs eRm | **1.00 / 1.00** |
| person-measure agreement (Pearson) vs eRm | **1.00** |
| person separation reliability | **0.86** |
| items calibrated | 24 |
| non-extreme persons calibrated (of 316) | 310 |

The substantive output is the **item hierarchy**
([`artifacts/item_hierarchy.csv`](artifacts/item_hierarchy.csv)): *want-to-curse*
items are easiest to endorse and *do-shout* items hardest — the established
VerbAgg ordering. For an ADL scale this is the clinically meaningful result:
which activities demand the most function (stairs, bathing) versus the least
(feeding).

## Conclusion

Scoring an ordinal ADL scale on its raw sum discards the fact that its steps are
unequal. A polytomous Rasch model recovers an interval measure and an
interpretable item hierarchy, and the ecosystem's dependency-free engine matches
the reference implementation exactly on real data. The transferable takeaway:
**before you compute change or an MCID on an ADL total, put it on an interval
scale — then equal gains mean equal gains.**

## Open questions

- Person separation reliability is 0.86 for 24 items; a shorter ADL scale
  (Barthel's 10 items, Katz's 6) separates persons less precisely, so the
  interval measure's per-person standard error — largest near the floor and
  ceiling — should be reported, not assumed uniform. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

The recipe is general: any set of ordinally-scored items measuring one construct.

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| recode instrument responses to Rasch categories | `raschRecode()` | PhysioClinical |
| fit the polytomous Rasch model, get the hierarchy | `raschAnalyze()` → `pcm_measure()` | PhysioClinical → PhysioAppKit |
| differential item functioning across groups | `pcm_dif()` | PhysioAppKit |
| concurrent calibration for pre/post change | `pcm_stack()` | PhysioAppKit |

They chain through a plain persons × items matrix. **Choosing the parameters:**
use the Partial Credit Model when items have different category structures (the
Barthel Index's mixed 0/5/10/15 weights) and the Rating Scale Model when every
item shares a format (all FIM items 1–7). Check the item hierarchy is
substantively sensible and that thresholds are ordered before trusting the
scale.

```r
library(PhysioClinical)
# a persons x items matrix of Barthel responses (weighted levels)
fit <- raschAnalyze("barthel", responses)     # -> interval measures + item hierarchy
fit$item_hierarchy                            # which ADLs demand the most function
# turn interval change into a responder verdict with the model's own SE:
raschResponder(pre_fit, post_fit, mcid = 0.5)
```

To apply it to your own hypothesis, register your instrument's items and call
`raschAnalyze()`; for cross-modal follow-up see the sibling ADL cases
(`adl-selfcare-hmp`) that add the *performance* side from wearable sensors.

One line for the technical reader: every number above traces to
[`artifacts/agreement.csv`](artifacts/agreement.csv) /
[`artifacts/item_hierarchy.csv`](artifacts/item_hierarchy.csv), re-checked by
[`audit.py`](audit.py) and the shared invariants in `tools/validate_case.py`.
